I’ve been thinking lately about the spaces we usually skip over: the hallway between rooms, the moment after a song ends but before the silence does, the blue light of 4:47 p.m. when the sun is still technically up but has already resigned. We build lives out of destinations—arrivals, conclusions, the neat click of a closing door—but we live almost entirely in the threshold.

A doorway is a strange architectural honesty. It admits that you are neither fully in nor fully out, that identity is just a matter of which side of the frame you’re leaning on right now. I like doors that are half-open, especially in old houses where the wood has warped slightly so the latch doesn’t quite catch and the whole thing breathes. There’s a negotiation happening in that gap: the room wants you; the hallway wants to keep you; you are just the air moving between them.

Twilight is the same. Not the grandeur of sunset, not the honesty of dark, but that suspended negotiation where colors forget their names. The sky stops being blue and starts being a question. I think consciousness is like that—less a spotlight and more a long, slow dissolve between what was just thought and what is about to be. We think we’re fixed points, but we’re probably just weather patterns with opinions.

There’s a train in some city—maybe here, maybe there—that is always late, and people gather on the platform not because they want to leave, but because they’ve agreed to stand in a temporary community of not-yet. The platform is beautiful that way. No one asks where you’re going. They just ask if you’re okay with the wait.

I want to learn the grammar of waiting. Not the passive kind, the kind that feels like falling behind, but the active, architectural kind: the willingness to remain in a shape that hasn’t finished forming. To let a thought stay half-metaphor. To let a friendship exist in the long distance of letters and voice messages rather than demanding the resolution of a final dinner.

The world rewards endpoints. Careers culminate, relationships “get to the next level,” books have last pages. But I’m increasingly convinced that the interesting part is the draft—the version of you that exists only because the other version hasn’t arrived yet. The self that only exists in transit. The song that is still being composed by the noise of the street outside.

So I’ll stay here, in this unclaimed hour, writing without a conclusion. The words will do what they do: they’ll become a doorway. You can step through, or not. Either way, the light is changing, and that is enough.
